First multi-crew spaceflight — three cosmonauts in a Vostok-derived capsule

Voskhod 1 was the first flight to carry more than one person into space, and it managed it by subtraction. There was no room in the one-seat Vostok for a three-person crew, so the engineers took things out — the ejection seats that had saved every previous cosmonaut, and, because even then it was too tight, the pressure suits. Komarov, Feoktistov, and Yegorov flew for a day in shirtsleeves, with no way to escape a launch or reentry emergency and no protection if the cabin lost air. Nothing went wrong, so it looked like a triumph. It was really a bet — that the corners cut to score a first wouldn't be the ones that mattered — and it happened to win.

First three-crew spaceflight in history. Komarov, Feoktistov and Yegorov flew 1964-10-12 to 1964-10-13 in a heavily modified Vostok capsule (designated Voskhod / 'Sunrise'). Ejection seats were removed and the cabin pressure system re-rated to allow three men to sit in shirtsleeves — a propaganda victory against the planned US Gemini two-crew flights, but a brutal compromise that left the crew with no escape capability during launch or re-entry. Landed 1964-10-13 07:47 UTC in northern Kazakhstan, about 312 km north-east of Kostanay, using the new soft-landing solid-rocket retro system because no parachute ejection was possible. Khrushchev was ousted just after they landed; the crew were welcomed home by a new Soviet leadership.
Soft-landing retro-rocket touchdown in northern Kazakhstan, about 312 km north-east of Kostanay, 1964-10-13 07:47 UTC.
Khrushchev was removed from power on 13–14 October, just after the landing.
